name: Tetrahydrozoline drops (Visine)
lead: Tetrahydrozoline (also spelled tetryzoline) is an over-the-counter vasoconstrictor used in eye drops and nasal sprays. The best-known redness-relief eye drop containing it is Visine, which contains 0.05 percent tetrahydrozoline hydrochloride and is sold to temporarily relieve eye redness from minor irritations.[1][2] By narrowing the small blood vessels on the surface of the eye, it makes the whites (sclera) look whiter and clearer within minutes, which is why people use it before photos, interviews or dates to make eyes look brighter and more rested.[1][2]

In looksmaxxing communities such drops are discussed as a quick way to whiten the sclera and brighten the eyes. Reference sources note that tetrahydrozoline is not meant for prolonged use because tolerance can develop and stopping it can cause rebound redness [1], and forum users themselves frequently mention rebound as a drawback and compare it unfavorably with brimonidine-based drops [3]. Accidental or deliberate oral ingestion can cause serious poisoning, particularly in children [1].

paras: Tetrahydrozoline is used to relieve redness of the eye from minor irritants, and can be combined with antazoline for allergic conjunctivitis [1]. Visine redness products carry 0.05 percent tetrahydrozoline hydrochloride and, per Grokipedia, fall under the US FDA over-the-counter monograph for ophthalmic drugs as safe and effective for short-term relief of redness from minor irritation. Other Visine lines contain lubricants such as polyethylene glycol or hypromellose, or antihistamines for allergy symptoms [2].
In looksmaxxing forums, users describe using redness drops to make the whites of the eyes look clearer, usually as a short-term measure [3].

sections.h: Why the whites of the eyes look whiter
paras: The sclera is a tough, collagen-rich white coat of the eyeball, covered by a thin membrane called the conjunctiva. The blood vessels of the conjunctiva and the underlying episclera are what make an irritated eye look red.[18] Because the whiteness of the sclera is a strong contrast against the iris, redness-free eyes are often read as brighter, healthier and more rested, which is the appearance goal behind redness drops.

Redness drops work on that visible vessel layer. Tetrahydrozoline narrows the vessels, so less blood shows through the conjunctiva and the eye looks whiter within minutes.[1][2] The drops do not change the sclera itself. Wikipedia notes that natural tint differences in the sclera exist, such as a faint blue cast in children, a yellowish tone with age from fatty deposits, and yellowing in jaundice, and these are not vessel-related.[18]

Tetrahydrozoline is an alpha-adrenergic agonist acting on alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors, which constricts blood vessels in the eye; its biological half-life in healthy people is about 6 hours, with part excreted unchanged in urine [1]. Grokipedia describes the effect as beginning within minutes and localized to conjunctival vessels at normal use [2].

Visine formulations vary: the original line uses tetrahydrozoline, while other versions use oxymetazoline or naphazoline, some combined with the antihistamine pheniramine.[9] Brimonidine, a selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist sold in low-dose OTC redness drops in the US, also constricts blood vessels and appears in looksmaxxing discussion as an alternative to tetrahydrozoline.[3][10] Wikipedia lists common brimonidine eye side effects as itchiness, redness and dry mouth.[10] The forum comparisons of rebound between the two come from user reports; no published head-to-head trial of rebound between the two was found.[3]

Redness-relief drops fall into a few families. Tetrahydrozoline, oxymetazoline and naphazoline are older imidazoline vasoconstrictors, while brimonidine at a low concentration is sold under the brand name Lumify as a redness reliever.[9][10][19] Wikipedia describes brimonidine as an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist whose peripheral alpha-2 activity narrows blood vessels.[10][19] Lubricating drops such as those containing polyethylene glycol or hypromellose address dryness rather than vessel size.[2]

In looksmaxxing discussion, Visine is usually treated as the classic quick-fix option and brimonidine drops as the newer alternative that users say rebounds less.[3] These comparisons come from user reports; no published head-to-head trial of rebound is available.

Wikipedia states that the drug is not intended for prolonged use because its effect wears off; after tolerance develops, stopping it can cause rebound vasodilation and more redness, and prolonged nasal use can cause rebound congestion [1]. Eye drops may cause blurred vision, irritation and pupil dilation [1]. Product labeling, as described by Grokipedia, advises consulting a doctor for persistent symptoms and cautions that overuse can cause rebound redness, eye pain or vision changes, and recommends removing contact lenses before use [2].

Oral ingestion of tetrahydrozoline can cause slowed heart rate, respiratory depression, low blood pressure, drowsiness and vomiting, and children are the most common overdose victims. There is no antidote and treatment is supportive; fatalities are rare with treatment [1]. Wikipedia also reports the substance has been involved in criminal cases of drugging, and notes that a popular belief about it causing violent diarrhea does not reflect the actual range of effects [1]. A published case report examined drug-facilitated sexual assault involving a tetrahydrozoline eye drop [4].

Wikipedia's Visine article notes that stinging and burning can occur on application, that the rebound effect can make redness worse, and that prolonged use can leave vessels dilated; it also says some formulas are not advised for contact lens wearers or for people with glaucoma.[9] In a 2005 double-blind trial of 50 computer users with eye discomfort, 28 percent (7 of 25) of those using Visine Original reported temporary stinging or burning after instillation, compared with 4 percent (1 of 24) using a polysorbate-80 lubricant.[13]

Ingestion cases are documented in the medical literature. A 2003 case report and review described neurological and cardiovascular complications in a child who accidentally swallowed Visine and noted the product is not sold in childproof containers.[12] Case reports describe an adult with haemodynamic compromise after a Visine overdose and a complete atrioventricular block after ingestion.[14][15] A 2024 scoping review of 15 articles on non-medical uses found the most common clinical presentation was unexplained, resistant slow heart rate and low blood pressure.[11] Wikipedia advises that ingestion warrants immediate medical attention or a call to a poison control center.[9]

Tetrahydrozoline was patented in 1954 and entered medical use in 1959 [1]. Visine was introduced by Leeming in the late 1950s (Grokipedia gives both 1957 and 1958), came under Pfizer after the company acquired Leeming in 1961, passed to Johnson & Johnson in 2006 and to Kenvue in 2023 [2]. Some Grokipedia details are not corroborated elsewhere and its dates are inconsistent.
Older toxicology research has also examined Visine as an adulterant in urine drug-screen testing and reported effects on cannabinoid immunoassays [5][6].

Wikipedia's Visine article gives 1958 as the year of introduction, says Pfizer acquired the brand in 1999 and that Johnson & Johnson acquired it in 2006 with Pfizer's consumer healthcare portfolio; this differs from the Grokipedia account of Leeming and a 1961 Pfizer acquisition, so ownership dates vary between sources.[2][9] The article also notes cultural references such as the film Wedding Crashers, which it says misrepresents the effects of swallowing Visine, and criminal cases in which Visine was alleged to have been used to poison victims, including a 2018 South Carolina case and a 2019 North Carolina case.[9] A 2023 forensic nursing case report documents a drug-facilitated sexual assault involving tetrahydrozoline given rectally.[17]

On looksmax.org, a poster describes using redness drops to make eyes look lighter and proposes alternating tetrahydrozoline and brimonidine drops to avoid tolerance and mask rebound, while a reply says Visine is stronger and causes rebound redness, making it counterproductive [3]. The poster states that eye health is being set aside for the effect. These are user opinions without clinical testing.

No studies found of tetrahydrozoline as a cosmetic eyewhitening treatment. Related published work includes a randomized comparison of Systane UD drops versus Visine Intensiv for moderate dry eye [7], and a case report of a nonpigmenting fixed drug eruption linked to tetrahydrozoline sensitivity [8].

A 2005 randomised double-blind trial in 50 healthy adults with computer-related eye discomfort compared Visine Original with a lubricant eye drop for five days and found similar symptom relief between them.[13] A 2012 trial of contact lens-related dry eye used Visine for Contacts rewetting drops as the comparator for azithromycin drops.[16] These studies are about comfort, not cosmetic whitening.

timeline.event: Wikipedia gives this as the year Visine was introduced; Grokipedia gives 1957 or 1958.[2][9]
Case report and review of a child's accidental Visine ingestion is published, noting the product is not sold in childproof containers.[12]
Randomised trial in 50 computer users compares Visine Original with a lubricant drop.[13]
Johnson & Johnson acquires Visine in its purchase of Pfizer's consumer healthcare business.[2]
Visine transfers to Kenvue after the Johnson & Johnson consumer health spin-off.[2]
Forensic nursing case report on drug-facilitated assault with tetrahydrozoline is published; a 2024 scoping review follows on its non-medical uses.[17][11]

lore.intro: Forum users mention Visine as a redness drop for whiter sclera and contrast it with Lumify, citing rebound redness as its main drawback [3].

claims.claim: Redness drops with tetrahydrozoline whiten the eyes quickly.
claims.believers: A poster says tetrahydrozoline constricts eye vessels to make them white [3].
claims.experts: Tetrahydrozoline is an alpha-adrenergic agonist that constricts ocular vessels and is approved over the counter for short-term redness relief [1][2].

claims.claim: Visine causes rebound redness and is stronger than Lumify.
claims.believers: A reply in a forum thread states that Visine is stronger and causes rebound redness, and the original poster says Lumify rebounds less [3].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that stopping tetrahydrozoline after tolerance develops can cause rebound redness [1]; no study compares it directly with brimonidine for rebound.

claims.claim: Alternating Visine and Lumify avoids tolerance.
claims.believers: A poster proposes alternating the two drops on different days to avoid tolerance and mask rebound effects [3].
claims.experts: No published study has tested alternating regimens of different redness drops; labels advise consulting a doctor for persistent redness [2].

claims.claim: Redness drops make eyes look more rested for photos and events.
claims.believers: Forum users describe using the drops shortly before being seen so the whites look clear and contrasted against the iris.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia explains that redness comes from conjunctival and episcleral vessels, which vasoconstrictors narrow; the effect on appearance has not been studied as a cosmetic outcome.[18][1]

claims.claim: Brimonidine drops are gentler than tetrahydrozoline.
claims.believers: A poster says brimonidine drops rebound less and prefers them, while another says Visine is stronger.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists brimonidine's common eye side effects as itchiness, redness and dry mouth; no published trial compares rebound between the two drops.[10][19]

card.summary: OTC redness drops (0.05% tetrahydrozoline) that whiten the sclera fast, with well-known rebound redness on repeated use.
card.note: Rebound redness with prolonged use; oral ingestion is dangerous, especially for children.

quick.overview:
Visine-type drops contain tetrahydrozoline, a vasoconstrictor that shrinks surface blood vessels in the eye to reduce redness. Looksmaxxers use them for whiter sclera.
The redness-relief effect is established and the product is sold over the counter for short-term use. Reference sources describe rebound redness after prolonged use, and no study has examined it as a cosmetic treatment.
quick.mechanism: Tetrahydrozoline is an alpha-adrenergic agonist acting on alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors, constricting vessels on the eye surface. Effects start within minutes and its half-life is about 6 hours.
quick.risks: Prolonged use can lead to tolerance and rebound redness, and eye drops may cause blurred vision, irritation and dilated pupils. Swallowing the product can cause serious poisoning, especially in children, with no antidote. Labels advise seeing a doctor for persistent redness and removing contact lenses first.

chain: Drops applied to the eye surface
Less visible redness, whiter-looking whites within minutes
angle.text: Redness drops reduce visible blood vessels in the sclera so the eyes look whiter and brighter for several hours. Forum users use them as a short-term cosmetic measure, typically before photos or events.
